terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where Idris's price list quotes three papers, and every failure lands in one catch().

tasks.title: A throw in a callback
tasks.description:
When `onFulfilled` or `onRejected` throws, the docket from `then()` fails with exactly what was thrown.

- the throw goes no further: `resolve`, `reject` and `then()` never throw because a callback did
- one callback that throws does not stop the other callbacks waiting on the same docket
- this holds on a docket that settles later and on one already settled

The check gives dockets of its own callbacks that throw, settles them, and reads the docket from `then()` and anything that escaped.
nextSteps: Run `node src/price-list.js`: it stops on `catch()`, which is task 2. Press Check to see where a throw in a callback goes today.
Find the one place where a callback is called.
Catch what it throws there, and fail the docket from `then()` with it.
Run the script again: it now stops at `catch()`, which is the next task.
hints: Whoever called `resolve` (the code that read a file, a timer) has no idea a callback is waiting, and cannot do anything sensible with its error. The docket from `then()` is the one place the error belongs.
A `try` around the callback call catches it. In the `catch`, the docket from `then()` has a function for exactly this.
`try { const result = callback(this.value); /* settle as before */ } catch (error) { reject(error) }`, where `reject` belongs to the docket `then()` returns.

tasks.title: catch()
tasks.description:
Implement `catch(onRejected)` in `src/docket.js`. It works like `then(undefined, onRejected)`.

- it returns a new docket
- on a failure, `onRejected(reason)` runs once, and the new docket is kept with what it returned, so the chain carries on; a returned docket is waited for, as with `onFulfilled`
- on a docket that is kept, `onRejected` does not run and the new docket is kept with the same value
- `then(undefined, onRejected)` behaves the same way: what `onRejected` returns keeps the docket from `then()`

The check uses `catch()` and `then(undefined, handler)` on dockets of its own that fail or are kept, and reads the new docket.
nextSteps: Look at what `then()` does today after `onRejected` has run.
Make `onRejected`'s result settle the new docket the same way `onFulfilled`'s does.
Run the script: the poster and napkin lines should now say why there is no quote.
hints: `catch()` is not a new idea, only a shorter way to write a `then()` with no `onFulfilled`. All the work is in `then()`.
Today `then()` treats the two callbacks differently: one's result keeps the next docket, the other's is thrown away. A handler that dealt with the failure has finished its step like any other.
`catch(onRejected) { return this.then(undefined, onRejected) }`, and in `then()` pick the callback by state, then settle the new docket from its result the same way for both.

tasks.title: A failure skips ahead
tasks.description:
Make a failure travel down a chain to the first callback that takes it.

- when `onRejected` is missing or not a function, the docket from `then()` fails with the same reason, unchanged
- no `onFulfilled` runs on the way
- this holds for a docket that failed, one that fails later, and a throw in an earlier callback

The check builds chains of `then()` calls with only `onFulfilled`, ending in `then(undefined, handler)`, and records what ran and how a docket in the middle ended. This task builds on task 1; the check says so when it is not done.
nextSteps: Look at the napkin quote: its count fails, and two `then()` calls stand between it and `catch()`.
Find what `then()` does today when the docket failed and there is no `onRejected`.
Pass the failure on to the docket from `then()`, the way a missing `onFulfilled` passes a value on.
Run the script: every line should end in a quote or a reason.
hints: A step that has nothing to do with the failure must not swallow it. The next docket has to fail too, or the failure is lost.
You already pass a value on when there is no `onFulfilled`. A missing `onRejected` is the same idea for the other state.
When the matching callback is not a function: `kept ? resolve(this.value) : reject(this.value)`.
